text:
Healey says people living in council tax A to D band homes to get £100 energy payment
Healey says people living in homes in council tax bands A to D will get a £100 energy payment this winter.
That will help 20m households, he says.
Let me say this to families at home. I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space.
So today I’m taking one further step this winter.
For 20 million households in council tax bands A to D, I’m announcing a £100 energy payment for households.
Healey says he investing in civil service transformation, launching a review of NHS productivity, “reducing the double running between central and local government” and setting up a local apprenticeships service.
Healey says he is delivering most radical act of fiscal devolution in generation
And Healey announces more powers for mayors.
In today’s budget I’m announcing new good growth funds for mayors and incubator capital for areas without mayors.
I’m announcing flexible funding to invest in local economies, boosted by a further £1.5bn of devolved loans for mayor authorities, funds that will back projects like the new Black Country metro extension led by the mayor of the West Midlands, or the urban regeneration in Gateshead …
This is unfinished business for me. As a Treasury minister in the last Labour government, I was proud to help create the regional development agencies. They delivered economic growth, local regeneration before they were axed in 2010 by the Tory Lib Dem coalition.
But there is a further step we never took – the most radical act of devolution in a generation. The devolution of tax revenues.
That is the step I take today. Alongside this budget, a roadmap for fiscal devolution. For the first time, I’m making the commitment that 100% of business rates will be retained locally by the end of the decade.
So if local leaders help businesses to start and grow, more of the rates they pay will stay in that area. Fom next year 20% of business rates revenues will go to mayors and, from 2028, a share of income tax receipts will go to mayors as well.
Also, from 2028, mayors and other strategic authorities will have new powers to introduce an overnight visitors levy.
Taken together, these are long-term funding streams they can be used to back investment into big local infrastructure, so that more of the money that is raised locally can be invested and spent locally.
Healey announces new tax relief for people who set up successful firms
Healey announces a tax cut to help people setting up their own business.
I know starting a company means taking a risk, often leaving a secure job and build something that there’s no guarantee will work. A
And I believe that when business founders take that risk, build an exceptional company, create wealth for Britain, we should recognise that success and keep those people here to invest again.
That is why today I’m announcing a founder’s relief, a brand new relief in capital gains tax, a 10% rate on lifetime gains, up to £10m for the founders of our most successful firms.
I’m setting out a new deal for datacentres in the UK. When the NHS uses AI to treat patients, we want that data here. When our armed forces unit use AI to keep us safe, we want that data here.
So here’s the deal.
I’m today launching a new British datacentre covenant with strict tests that datacentres must meet to invest in local communities, create local jobs and protect local water supplies.
In return, critical datacentres will get the grid connections they need and, where necessary, be allowed to build onsite generation while they wait.
This £20.4bn of additional funding for the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund shows that John Healey is taking advantage of a change made by predecessor Rachel Reeves.
Reeves switched the measure of the UK national debt to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities (PSNFL), which subtracts liquid and illiquid financial assets from the UK’s financial liabilities.
That means extra borrowing to fund these public financial institutions (PuFins) doesn’t make it harder to keep within the fiscal rules.
Clever? Perhaps. But there’s a risk that bond investors will be suspicious that the chancellor is hiding some of the government’s borrowing.
Consultancy OxfordEconomics warned in August:
Chancellor John Healey will present his first UK Budget on October 28, and there have been strong rumours he plans to increase spending by public financial institutions or PuFins. This would be an accounting trick to raise investment within the fiscal rules. But it would increase the government’s financing needs and risks undermining its fiscal credibility.
Healey announces a £20.4bn boost for investment in the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank over the coming years, supporting 140,000 jobs.
And he says he is bringing back the Better Regulation Executive, that was scrapped by the Tories “to cut outdated regulations and admin burdens on business”.
Bank stocks are pushing higher, after Healey confirmed that the extra taxes on the sector will be lower than had been expected (see previous post).
Today’s decision to lift the bank surcharge by 3 percentage points (so, up from 3% to 6%, we assume) means it will not return to the 8% level at which it operated before Jeremy Hunt lowered it in 2023.
NatWest are up almost 4%, and Lloyds are 3.75% higher, adding to their earlier gains.
Investors may also be relieved that the surcharge will only last 15 months, once it starts in January.
This surcharge is levied on top of corporation tax.
Campaigners for a bank tax will surely be disappointed that the chancellor hasn’t gone further.
The TUC had been pushing for a higher surcharge - suggesting 16%, or even 35%, would be appropriate.
The big four banks posted combined profits of £46 billion last year after several years of high interest rates – £13 billion (41%) a year higher than when rates were at near-zero in 2021, they pointed out.
Healey announces 3% rise in bank surcharge, but time-limited for just 15 months
Turning to banks, Healey says:
Our world leading banks make a huge contribution to this country in the tax they pay in the jobs industry and investment they support.
As chancellor, I want to say directly to our banks: I celebrate and I am grateful for the role that you play.
Amid the global economic storms, I am looking to our banks to help fund breathing space for British families.
And so banks will pay an extra 3% on the bank surcharge. This will be time limited to pay for immediate support on energy bills, starting in January, ending 15 months later.
He challenges the Tories to say if they will support this.
Healey says he is providing “greater upfront relief for new investment” and “reducing the threshold for business asset disposal relief in capital gains tax from £1m to £500,000.
He says the tax on income from property and savings will go up by two percentage points from April 2027.
And he confrms that he is scrapping the plan to reduce the Isa cash allowance.
I will not go ahead with the cut to the tax free amount that people can put into a cash Isa. The limit will stay at £20,000 per year, tax free for people of all ages to make investment more accessible.
Third, I am modernising the tax treatment of investment by foreign sovereigns. This will bring UK rules more in line with other investment and other nations, while remaining still one of the world’s most generous regimes in the world.
And fourth, I will resolve the question of VAT for larger taxed companies, ensuring they play by the same rules no matter where they’re located, while still protecting smaller local firms.
Healey says he is changing some business tax rules.
I’m changing outdated rules so that people taking profits out of their companies are taxed consistently, and I will protect the treatment of genuine commercial transactions and families passing their businesses down to the next generation.
I’m giving HMRC funding to improve compliance and stronger powers to collect overdue tax from those who can clearly afford to pay but ignore repeated contact.
And I’m reforming the administration of self-assessment income tax from 2029, bringing more of these taxpayers in line with the majority so that they make smaller, more regular payments instead of facing large bills that are often harder to pay.
Healey confirms that the government is raising the minimum wage by 3.9%.
The Treasury explains this will raise the National Living Wage to £13.21 an hour and the 18-20 National Minimum Wage to £11.27.
This rise was reported earlier this week, and led to accusations that Labour was breaking a manifesto pledge to raise the minimum wage for younger people up to the level that applies to workers over the age of 21.
digest_he: שר העסקים הבריטי, ג'ונתן ריינולדס, דרש הבהרות מבעלי רשת חנויות ההוזלה פאונדלנד, חברת ההשקעות האמריקאית גורדון בראדרהרט, על רקע דיווחים לפיהם הרשת בדרך למנות מנהלים מיוחדים לקראת חדלות פירעון. המהלך מגיע לאחר שהבעלים דחו הצעה לרכישת החברה כולה כמפעל חיים מצד קבוצת משקיעים. הממשלה הביעה דאגה עמוקה לגורלם של 12 אלף עובדי הרשת, בזמן שגורמים בשוק מעריכים כי החברה עשויה להיות מפורקת ונכסיה יימכרו לחברות שונות במקום להימכר כמקשה אחת.
